questions.answerExplanation:
(a) The title is 32px and the menu is shown. The screen is wider than 600px, so the rules inside the media query do not apply.
(b) The title is 20px and the menu is hidden. The screen is 600px or narrower, so the rules inside the media query apply and override the earlier rules.
(c) It tells the phone to use its real screen width for the page instead of pretending to be a wide desktop screen and zooming out. Without it, the phone may not match max-width: 600px, so the mobile styles would not apply.

questions.question:
A student uses browser dev tools to work out why their page is broken.
(a) The student selects a heading in the Elements panel. In the Styles pane, their rule `color: red` is shown with a line through it. What does the line mean, and how can they find out which rule is actually setting the colour?
(b) The student fixes the colour by editing it directly in the Styles pane, and the page looks right. When they reload the page, the fix is gone. Why, and what should they do?
questions.answerExplanation:
(a) The line means the declaration matched the element but was overridden by another rule, for example one with higher specificity or one that comes later. They can look for the rule higher up in the Styles pane that is not crossed out, or open the Computed tab to see the final colour and which rule it came from.
(b) Changes made in dev tools only affect the copy of the page currently open in the browser. They are not saved to the student's CSS file, so reloading loads the original file again. They need to make the same change in their CSS file and save it.

questions.knowledgePoint: CSS 选择器与层叠优先级
questions.answerExplanation:
(a) Red. An id selector (#intro) has higher specificity than a class selector, which has higher specificity than a type selector, so the id rule wins regardless of order.
(b) Green. Both `.note` and `p` match the element, and with the id rule gone the class selector has the higher specificity.
(c) `!important` breaks the normal cascade, so later readers (and future you) cannot override a rule with custom CSS. It is fine for a very small number of utility overrides but should not be used to win specificity fights.

(a) 300 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 5 = 350px. With content-box the declared width only covers the content, so padding and border are added on top.
(b) With border-box the 300px includes padding and border, so the content area shrinks and the total width stays 300px.
(c) Use rem when the size should scale with the user's root font size (better for accessibility), e.g. body or heading text. Use px for things that should stay fixed regardless of user settings, like a 1px border.

(a) On a row (default) flex container, justify-content spreads children along the main axis (horizontally), while align-items aligns them along the cross axis (vertically).
(b) Add `flex-direction: column;` and change the alignment, e.g. `align-items: center;` to centre horizontally and `justify-content: center;` for the vertical axis.
(c) `flex: 1` lets the child grow and shrink to fill the free space, so siblings share the leftover width proportionally.

(a) Two columns. The free space is split into 3 parts; the first column gets 1 part (~1/3) and the second gets 2 parts (~2/3).
(b) `gap` adds consistent space between rows and columns without margins, so the layout does not depend on margin collapsing or gutters on edge items.
(c) A framework or utility layer provides a consistent, documented set of primitives (spacing, layout, components), which speeds up development and keeps spacing and responsive behaviour consistent across a team.

(a) An absolutely positioned element is positioned relative to its nearest ancestor that is not `position: static`. Setting `.card` to `position: relative` makes it that ancestor, so the badge's `top`/`right` are measured from the card, not the whole page.
(b) z-index controls stacking order among positioned elements on the same level. It does nothing when the element is `static`, or when the elements are in different stacking contexts (for example a parent with its own z-index or opacity), which is the usual reason it 'does not work'.
(c) `relative` keeps the element in the normal flow and offsets it from its own original position; `absolute` takes it out of the flow and positions it against its containing block, so it no longer reserves space.

questions.question: A product card is inside a 320px column. The card rule declares `width: 300px`, plus 20px padding and 3px border on each side. What is the card's real total width, why does it overflow, and what changes if `.card` gets `box-sizing: border-box`?
questions.answerExplanation: Without `border-box`, the declared width is only the content box, so the total width is `300 + 40 + 6 = 346px`, which overflows the 320px column by 26px. With `box-sizing: border-box`, the declared 300px includes padding and border, so the total width becomes 300px and the content area shrinks instead of the whole card growing.

questions.question: A toolbar is `display: flex`, `justify-content: space-between`, `align-items: center`, and stays 600px by 160px. If `flex-direction` changes from `row` to `column`, where do the three buttons move, and which property should change if the designer wants them packed at the top but still centred horizontally?
questions.answerExplanation: Changing to `column` makes the main axis vertical, so `justify-content: space-between` spreads the buttons from top to bottom while `align-items: center` keeps them centred horizontally. To pack them at the top, change `justify-content` to `flex-start` (or `start`).

questions.question: A green button is matched by `button`, `.action`, `button.action`, and `#panel .action`. Why does the id-based rule beat the later `button.action` rule, and what colour wins if `id="panel"` is removed from the markup?
questions.answerExplanation: The id-based selector wins because specificity is compared before source order. `#panel .action` includes an id, so it beats `button.action` even if the latter is later in the stylesheet. If the id is removed, that rule stops matching and `button.action` becomes the winning rule, so the button turns blue.
